q: Explain the software process and why we build models.
a: The software process is a structured set of activities: specification, design and implementation, validation (testing) and maintenance/evolution. A model is an abstraction of a system that lets us ignore unessential details. We build models to reduce complexity, test the system before building it, communicate with the customer and document and visualize ideas.

Functional diagrams (use case) describe functionality from the user's view; static diagrams (class, object, package) describe static structure; dynamic diagrams include interaction diagrams (object interactions), state diagrams (behavior of an individual object over time) and activity diagrams (workflow).

q: What is object-oriented software and what are its main characteristics?
a: OO software organizes software as a collection of discrete objects that incorporate both data structure and behavior; the fundamental unit is the object with state and operations (unlike structured programming where data and operations were separate). Characteristics: identity, classification, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, generics, cohesion and coupling.

Identity: every object has its own identity (memory address/handle) even if two objects have identical state. Classification: objects with the same attributes and operations belong to the same class, which is an abstraction relevant to the application. Abstraction: selective examination of certain aspects of a problem, isolating what is important for the purpose (e.g. a Car for the DMV vs for a mechanic).

Encapsulation separates the external aspects of an object from its internal implementation details through data hiding and implementation hiding. It reduces interdependency: for example, the sort() operation of a List class can change from Bubble Sort to Quick Sort without affecting applications using the class.

q: Explain inheritance and polymorphism with examples.
a: Inheritance shares attributes and operations among classes in a hierarchy: a superclass holds general features and subclasses inherit and refine them (e.g. Car with Taxi and Truck). Polymorphism means the same operation behaves differently in different classes: getArea() is length x width in Rectangle, pi x radius squared in Circle and side squared in Square; each class's implementation is a method.

q: Describe the class model and the class notation.
a: The class model captures static structure: classes/objects, their relationships, and attributes and operations. A class is a box with up to three compartments (name, attributes, operations). An attribute is a named property with a value in each object; an operation is a function applied to objects and a method is its implementation. A missing compartment means not yet specified, an empty one means none exist.

q: How would you identify the classes in the flights system?
a: Classes appear as common nouns in the description: City, Airport, Airline, Flight, Passenger, Seat, Plane, Pilot (and Co-Pilot).
